method: OPEN AND QUOTED, from the RCH Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline 'CSF interpretation' (Last updated October 2024), retrieved 2026-09-23. Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: Free to read but NOT openly licensed -- each page carries '(c) 2026 The Royal Children's Hospital'. Quoted with attribution on the same footing as the 14 RCH guidelines and the Immunisation Handbook guidelines already in this compendium.

claims.claim: ⚠️ **If CSF is abnormal, the safest option is to start empiric antimicrobials for bacterial meningitis.**
claims.source_text: If CSF is abnormal, the safest option is to commence empiric antimicrobial treatment for bacterial meningitis
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'CSF interpretation' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/csf/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Any neutrophils in the CSF, at any age, may indicate bacterial meningitis** — discuss with a senior clinician.
claims.source_text: The presence of any neutrophils in the CSF, regardless of age, may indicate bacterial meningitis. Discussion with a senior clinician is recommended
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'CSF interpretation' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/csf/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **CSF values vary with age**: white cell count and protein are higher at birth and fall over the first 2 weeks of life.
claims.source_text: CSF parameters vary with age, which influences how a sample is interpreted … CSF white cell count and protein level are higher at birth and fall in the first 2 weeks of life
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'CSF interpretation' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/csf/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Meningitis can occur with normal CSF microscopy.** With high clinical suspicion, **treat with IV antimicrobials anyway** pending cultures or PCR.
claims.source_text: Meningitis can occur in children with normal CSF microscopy … If there is a high clinical suspicion of meningitis or encephalitis, children who have a normal CSF microscopy should still be treated with IV antimicrobials, pending cultures or PCR
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'CSF interpretation' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/csf/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Under 1 month:** protein under 1.0 g/L; CSF:blood glucose ratio 0.6 or more (or glucose 2.0 mmol/L or more); lactate 0.9–2.5 mmol/L. **Over 1 month:** protein under 0.4 g/L; glucose ratio 0.6 or more (or 2.5 mmol/L or more); lactate 1.0–2.0 mmol/L.
claims.source_text: Protein (g/L) Glucose CSF:blood ratio (total) Lactate (mmol/L) <1 month 0# <22 <1.0 ≥0.6 (or ≥2.0 mmol/L) 0.9-2.5 >1 month 0 ≤5 <0.4 ≥0.6 (or ≥2.5 mmol/L) 1.0-2.0
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'CSF interpretation' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/csf/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Neonates:** up to 5% of CSF white cells in neonates without meningitis can be neutrophils.
claims.source_text: Note: # Some studies have found that up to 5% of white blood cells in the CSF of neonates without meningitis, comprise neutrophils
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'CSF interpretation' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/csf/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Bacterial meningitis:** protein over 1.0 g/L, CSF:blood glucose ratio under 0.4, lactate over 2.0 mmol/L — **over 4.0 is strongly predictive**. Each value may be normal.
claims.source_text: Protein (g/L) Glucose (CSF:blood ratio) Lactate (mmol/L) Bacterial meningitis 100-10,000* <100 >1.0* <0.4* >2.0* (>4.0 is strongly predictive of bacterial meningitis) … Note: *may be normal
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'CSF interpretation' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/csf/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Viral meningitis:** protein 0.4–1.0 g/L, glucose usually normal, lactate under 2.0 mmol/L. **TB meningitis:** protein 1.0–5.0 g/L, glucose ratio under 0.3, lactate over 2.0 mmol/L.
claims.source_text: Protein (g/L) Glucose (CSF:blood ratio) Lactate (mmol/L) Bacterial meningitis … Viral meningitis <100 10-1000* 0.4-1.0* Usually normal <2.0 TB meningitis <100 50-1000* 1.0-5.0* <0.3* >2.0
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'CSF interpretation' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/csf/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Gram stain may be negative in up to 60% of bacterial meningitis**, even without prior antibiotics. **Lymphocyte predominance does not exclude bacterial meningitis**, and neutrophils may predominate in viral meningitis even after 24 hours.
claims.source_text: Gram stain may be negative in up to 60% of cases of bacterial meningitis, even without prior antibiotics … A predominance of lymphocytes does not exclude bacterial meningitis … Neutrophils may predominate in viral meningitis, even after the first 24 hours
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'CSF interpretation' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/csf/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Antibiotics given within 24 hours before LP are unlikely to alter cell count or biochemistry**, but usually prevent culture. Partially treated meningitis (recent oral antibiotics) may lower the neutrophil count.
claims.source_text: Antibiotics are unlikely to significantly affect the CSF cell count or biochemistry if the CSF sample was taken within 24 hours of antibiotic administration … Prior antibiotics usually prevent the culture of bacteria from the CSF … Partially treated meningitis (ie if the child has recently been on oral antibiotics) may result in a lower CSF neutrophil count than untreated bacterial meningitis
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'CSF interpretation' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/csf/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Seizures do not raise the CSF cell count.**
claims.source_text: Seizures do not cause an increased CSF cell count
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'CSF interpretation' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/csf/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Traumatic tap: count the total white cells and disregard the red cells.** If white cells exceed the normal range for age, **start empiric antibiotics**. Do not rely on correcting the white cell count for red cells.
claims.source_text: The safest interpretation of a traumatic tap is to count the total number of white cells and disregard the red cell count. If there are more white cells than the normal range for age, then the safest option is to commence empiric antibiotics … In the case of a traumatic tap, interpret CSF results with caution. Do not rely on correcting the CSF white cell count for the number of red cells
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'CSF interpretation' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/csf/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Some guidelines correct a traumatic tap** by 1 white cell per 500–700 red cells and 0.01 g/L protein per 1000 red cells — RCH advises against relying on this. Consider **subarachnoid haemorrhage** if red cells are unexplained or persistently raised.
claims.source_text: Some guidelines suggest that in traumatic taps, the white blood cell and protein count can be corrected based on the following calculation: 1 white blood cell for every 500-700 red blood cells and 0.01 g/L protein for every 1000 red cells … Do not rely on correcting the CSF white cell count for the number of red cells … Consider subarachnoid haemorrhage when there are unexplained or persistently elevated red blood cells in CSF
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'CSF interpretation' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/csf/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Analyse promptly**: neutrophils and lymphocytes fall progressively after 4 hours through cell lysis.
claims.source_text: Delays in laboratory analysis of CSF can alter cell counts as a result of lysis in the CSF. There is progressive reduction in both neutrophils and lymphocytes after 4 hours
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'CSF interpretation' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/csf/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **CSF PCR is widely available** for *N. meningitidis*, *S. pneumoniae*, HSV, enterovirus and parechovirus. Extended panels exist — interpret with caution (false positives) and correlate with the cell count.
claims.source_text: CSF PCR is widely available for Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, herpes simplex virus (HSV), enterovirus and parechovirus … Some health services have access to extended PCR panels … Interpret with caution due to potential false positives, and correlate with CSF cell count
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'CSF interpretation' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/csf/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Do not delay empiric treatment while waiting for PCR.** Meningococcal PCR is most useful after prior antibiotics.
claims.source_text: Do not delay empiric treatment while waiting for PCR results … Meningococcal PCR is particularly useful in patients with a clinical picture consistent with meningococcal meningitis, but who have received prior antibiotics
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'CSF interpretation' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/csf/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Request HSV PCR for suspected encephalitis** — it may be **negative in the first 36–72 hours**; repeat LP and HSV PCR after that if suspicion is high.
claims.source_text: HSV PCR should be requested for patients with clinical features of encephalitis. It may be negative in the first 36-72 hours of the illness. Consider repeating lumbar puncture and HSV PCR after this time if there is a high index of suspicion
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'CSF interpretation' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/csf/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Bacterial antigen tests should never influence treatment** — low sensitivity and specificity.
claims.source_text: CSF bacterial antigen tests have low sensitivity and specificity … They should therefore never influence treatment decisions and have little role if any in current management
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'CSF interpretation' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/csf/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Consult the local paediatric team** for all suspected encephalitis or bacterial meningitis, and any concern for non-infectious encephalopathy.
claims.source_text: Consider consultation with local paediatric team All children with suspected encephalitis or bacterial meningitis All children with concern for non-infectious encephalopathy
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'CSF interpretation' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/csf/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Consider transfer for** haemodynamic or respiratory instability, altered conscious state, seizures or focal signs, complications, or poor response to treatment.
claims.source_text: Consider transfer when Haemodynamic or respiratory instability Altered conscious state, seizures or focal neurological signs Child requiring care above the level of comfort of the local hospital Complications of meningitis or encephalitis or poor response to treatment
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'CSF interpretation' (Last updated October 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/csf/, retrieved 2026-09-23
